chunks: "A package-on-package chip is a stack of two packages. The bottom one is typically the processor, an application SoC, and its top surface has an array of solder-ball pads.
The top package is the memory, usually LPDDR DRAM, and its balls land on those pads. The whole stack is soldered to the board as one unit with the bottom package's balls.
The main benefits are board area and electrical performance.

The memory sits right above the SoC, so you save the footprint of a separate memory package, which in a phone is most of the area you'd spend on a memory chip plus its keep-out, and the interconnect between them is a millimetre or so of substrate instead of tens of millimetres of PCB trace.
That means lower delay, lower capacitance and lower I/O power, and it's easier to meet timing on a high-speed LPDDR bus.
It also lets a vendor mix and match: the same SoC with different memory sizes or suppliers. The trade-offs are mostly thermal and manufacturing.
The memory sits right on top of the hottest part, so the SoC's heat has to leave through the memory or down through the board, which makes the SoC run hotter and warms the DRAM.
The stack is taller, and the packages warp differently during reflow, which causes opens and shorts at the interface.
You also can't change the memory easily after assembly, rework is hard, and yield compounds: if either package is bad, you lose both unless you test before stacking.
And you're limited by the ball count and area of the interface, so for very high bandwidth you'd go to HBM and an interposer instead."
